summary: Describes a general JSON format for representing DNS messages, or parts of them. It is meant for tools that capture DNS queries and responses and want to search them or rebuild messages without decoding the binary wire format each time.

plainLanguage.summary: DNS messages are written in a secret code of bits. This gives them a plain, readable form so people and programs can look at them easily.

subtitle: Representing DNS messages in a human-readable JSON format.

tldr.problem: DNS messages are encoded as binary data on the wire, which makes them hard to search, analyze, or reconstruct without decoding the binary format each time.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8427 defines a JSON format that represents DNS message fields and resource records as JSON objects, allowing tools to exchange, store, and inspect DNS data in plain text while preserving the ability to reconstruct the original wire format.
tldr.outcome: Applications that capture DNS traffic or build DNS queries can use this format for logging, searching, and debugging without repeated binary encoding and decoding.

facts.label: Name encoding
facts.value: UTF-8 codepoints U+0000 to U+007F; IDNs in A-label form

facts.label: Data representation
facts.value: Multiple ways for same data (text and hex for names, decoded and raw for RDATA)

today: RFC 8427 is an Informational specification defining the JSON format for DNS messages and has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Introduction and Design Philosophy
sections.content:
DNS messages are defined in RFC 1035 as a binary wire format. This format is efficient for network transmission but difficult to search, log, or analyze without decoding the bits each time.

RFC 8427 specifies a JSON representation of DNS messages that preserves all the information from the binary format while making it human-readable and tool-friendly. The format is intentionally flexible: all members are optional, no object members are required, and profiles using this format can define their own requirements and add new members.

Key design principles include: the format allows transformation through JSON to recreate the wire content; members with 16-bit or shorter values are JSON numbers; the representation is limited to UTF-8 codepoints from U+0000 to U+007F to avoid encoding confusion; and the format explicitly allows description of malformed DNS messages, which is important for logging attack traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of writing DNS in secret code, write it in JSON, which is readable. You can pick the fields you care about, leave out the rest, and still recreate the original message if needed.

sections.title: DNS Message Structure in JSON
sections.content:
A DNS message in JSON is an object with optional members representing the message header and sections. Message header fields include ID (0 to 65535), QR (query vs. response), Opcode (0 to 15), flags (AA, TC, RD, RA, AD, CD), RCODE (response code, 0 to 15), and counts (QDCOUNT, ANCOUNT, NSCOUNT, ARCOUNT).

The Question section is represented by QNAME (the domain name being queried), QTYPE (query type, like A or AAAA), and QCLASS (usually IN for Internet). The Answer, Authority, and Additional sections each contain arrays of resource records, represented as objects with NAME, TYPE, CLASS, TTL, and RDATA fields. RDATA (resource record data) can be encoded as hexadecimal (RDATAHEX) or as structured fields for common types (rdataA for IPv4 addresses, rdataAAAA for IPv6 addresses, rdataCNAME, rdataNS, rdataTXT, etc.).

The same data can be represented multiple ways. For example, a domain name can appear as a plain string (NAME) or in hexadecimal (NAMEHEX), and message contents can be given as individual fields or as raw octets (messageOctetsHEX, headerOctetsHEX, etc.). This flexibility allows applications to choose representations that suit their needs.
sections.plainLanguage: A DNS message has a header (who is asking, what type of answer), a question (what domain to look up), and answers (what was found). JSON lets you write each part clearly with readable field names.

sections.title: Encoding and Name Handling
sections.content:
Names in DNS are encoded with length-prefixed labels. In JSON, names are represented as uncompressed domain names (after removing DNS compression from wire format). Fields ending in HEX are base16 encoded (hex with uppercase letters, as in RFC 4648).

Domain names use UTF-8 codepoints from U+0000 to U+007F, with labels separated by periods. Internationalized Domain Names (IDNs) are always expressed in their A-label form (ASCII Compatible Encoding). Fields that end in HEX contain the wire format of the name in hexadecimal, which is useful for systems that need to preserve the exact wire encoding.

A DNS message can also be represented as a paired query and response, using optional members queryMessage and responseMessage, each containing a message object. Streaming of multiple DNS objects is done using JSON text sequences (RFC 7464).
sections.plainLanguage: Domain names go in as text (like example.com.), or as hex code. You can have both in the same message so you can read it and also check the exact bytes that came from the wire.

sections.title: Profiles and Applications
sections.content:
RFC 8427 defines a general format, not a profile. Systems using this format will have their own policies about what members are mandatory, optional, or prohibited. For example, a passive DNS system (which logs DNS responses) might require QNAME, QTYPE, and answerRRs to be present. Another application that configures DNS test clients might allow all members to be optional and fill in missing values from previous records.

A media type application/dns+json is registered for this format. The specification allows any members to be included; receivers that do not understand extra members can simply ignore them, and profiles are expected to define constraints on what they use.
sections.plainLanguage: Different programs will use different parts of this format. A logger might track only questions and answers. A tester might fill in the header from a previous message and build a new query. This format supports all of that.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
A message object can inadvertently contain inconsistent data. For example, ANCOUNT might say 1 while answerRRs is empty, or an RDLENGTH might not match the decoded value in RDATAHEX. Readers must not assume that all fields are consistent with each other. The format explicitly supports representing malformed DNS messages, which is useful for logging attacks but requires careful validation.

Numbers in JSON have no inherent bounds. Integer values (ID, QR, RCODE, and so on) might have invalid values; for example, an ID greater than 65535 or a QR value of 2. Applications must validate these ranges themselves.

DNS data can contain privacy-sensitive information. For example, a profile logging DNS queries sent to recursive resolvers might capture source IP addresses that identify where a user is located. Applications should implement appropriate privacy and access control measures when handling this data.
sections.plainLanguage: JSON DNS messages might have weird or broken data in them (like saying there's 1 answer but showing 2). You have to check carefully. Also, DNS queries can reveal where someone is, so keep that data private.
